analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate the estate tax attracted 69 cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently eliminated the federal estate tax (the tax on large inheritances when someone dies), the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, effective after enactment [S2, S3]. The estate tax only applies to estates above a filing threshold, so its cost falls almost entirely on the heirs of the wealthiest households. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates, who would pay no federal tax on inheritances above the existing exemption. The ultra-wealthy would gain the most, since only estates exceeding the exemption amount owed any estate tax. Estate tax repeal would also reduce federal revenue that otherwise funds government programs.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire federal estate and gift tax structure (Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code), so no estate, gift, or generation-skipping transfer would be taxed after enactment [S3].
The repeal applies retroactively-forward to deaths, gifts, and transfers occurring after the date of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately taxpayers generally, would lose the revenue the estate tax raises, which falls almost entirely on the largest estates. Revenue lost from the estate tax would either add to deficits or have to be replaced by other taxes or spending cuts. Middle- and working-class families with small estates owed no estate tax and would see no direct tax benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers generally, via lost revenue

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax that applies only to the largest estates; under the law then in effect, estates could pass $5 million per person free of tax, so few families outside the top of the wealth distribution owed anything.
The federal government would permanently lose the revenue the estate tax raises, increasing deficits or forcing offsetting tax increases or spending cuts elsewhere [S3].

Supporters argue the tax forces surviving family members to sell farms and small businesses to pay the bill; critics respond that the $5 million-per-person exemption already exempted the vast majority of such estates, and that repeal primarily benefits very large fortunes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to heirs of very large estates, while its cost, lost federal revenue, is borne by everyone through deficits or other taxes. Because the exemption already protected most modest estates and family businesses, repeal is a large tax cut concentrated at the top with no direct benefit for the majority of households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on its introduction day and sat there; the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress, with 17 original cosponsors [S1, S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation, and that was its last action of record [S5].
The bill gathered 68 cosponsors (66 Republicans and 2 Democrats) but never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4, S5].
The bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without becoming law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal treasury were better off, since a permanent tax cut aimed at the largest estates never advanced. The estate tax, which only a small fraction of the wealthiest estates ever pays, remained in place. House Republicans who wanted repeal could point to their cosponsorship without having to schedule a vote that would have added to deficits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; large estates avoided a cut

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate and gift taxes on the first day of the 112th Congress.

for.name: 68 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the estate tax repeal, but no vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 5, 2011 and took no recorded action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, for the remaining two years of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 66 of 68 cosponsors were Republicans, with just 2 Democrats [S4], and the bill never advanced past referral in a Republican-led House.

industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated a tax that falls only on estates above the exemption threshold, sparing the largest inheritances. The lost revenue would be borne by taxpayers generally through deficits or offsetting taxes.
Repeal would reduce demand for estate and trust planning services built around the estate tax. This is a secondary, modest effect of the bill.
